problem: Characterize real numbers r such that floor(n r) has an infinite subsequence satisfying a homogeneous linear recurrence; seek negative-space hypotheses avoiding standard Beatty/Sturmian/continued-fraction approaches.

framings.reframing: Treat b_k = floor(n_k r) as the output of a scalar autonomous LTI system. Existence of a homogeneous recurrence means the infinite Hankel matrix built from b_k has finite rank and admits a Ho-Kalman style realization.
framings.key_insight: This shifts attention from word complexity to McMillan degree. A negative-space hypothesis is that for irrational r with no hidden algebraic renormalization, every admissible sampled trace has growing Hankel rank because the bounded carry term {n_k r} behaves like irreducible model error rather than finite-state dynamics.
framings.suggested_technique: Use finite Hankel-rank tests, vanishing Hankel minors, and Ho-Kalman or low-rank Hankel realization methods.
framings.mapping_back: If every candidate subsequence of floor(n r) has infinitely many nonzero Hankel minors, then no homogeneous recurrence exists. Conversely, any low-rank Hankel witness gives a concrete finite-dimensional algebraic model for the subsequence.

framings.reframing: Interpret a recurrent subsequence as a signal with an annihilating filter: after characteristic-root decomposition it is a finite sum of exponentials or polynomial-exponentials, exactly the regime of Prony, MUSIC, and ESPRIT.
framings.key_insight: Prony-type models are rigid. Since floor(n_k r) = r n_k - {n_k r}, the sampled data is a near-linear trend plus bounded phase noise, and sparse spectral methods suggest that only highly nongeneric sampling times could make this noise collapse into a finite pole set.
framings.suggested_technique: Apply Prony's method or annihilating-filter analysis to classify possible characteristic roots, then compare them with monotone near-linear growth.
framings.mapping_back: A successful recurrence would imply a finite pole set for b_k. Showing that the carry term forces broadband or non-annihilatable behavior rules out recurrent subsequences except in degenerate algebraic cases.

framings.reframing: Ask whether some extracted series G(z) = sum_{k>=0} floor(n_k r) z^k is rational. Homogeneous recurrences are exactly rational ordinary generating functions, and Kronecker or Hadamard machinery tests rationality via finite-rank Hankel structure and coefficientwise operations.
framings.key_insight: The negative-space heuristic is that irrational-slope floor data should produce sections with natural-boundary or nonrational singular behavior unless the extraction hides a very rigid algebraic pattern.
framings.suggested_technique: Use rationality criteria for power series, Kronecker finite-rank tests, and Hadamard quotient techniques.
framings.mapping_back: Instead of reasoning about words, prove that every admissible extracted generating series is nonrational. That immediately excludes homogeneous recurrences.

framings.reframing: View a putative recurrence as producing p-adically analytic zero conditions. Skolem-Mahler-Lech says zeros of linear recurrences are eventually finite unions of arithmetic progressions, and standard proofs pass through p-adic interpolation.
framings.key_insight: This suggests a negative-space hypothesis: if floor(n r) had a recurrent subsequence, the induced vanishing relations should force p-adic periodicity or semilinearity in the index set, something generic irrational rotations should resist.
framings.suggested_technique: Use p-adic interpolation, Strassmann-type arguments, and Skolem-Mahler-Lech reasoning on recurrence-derived difference sequences.
framings.mapping_back: Convert the recurrence into infinite vanishing of an auxiliary sequence built from floor(n_k r). If p-adic methods force eventual periodicity in k or n_k, compare that with the distribution of fractional parts {n r}.

framings.reframing: After characteristic-root decomposition, any recurrent subsequence is an exponential polynomial E_k with floor(n_k r) = E_k. Since E_k = r n_k + O(1), one gets infinitely many near-equalities between structured algebraic quantities and multiples of r.
framings.key_insight: This replaces continued fractions by multiplicative dependence. Baker-Wustholz bounds and the Subspace Theorem are built to show that repeated near-cancellations among algebraic exponentials only happen when hidden algebraic relations exist.
framings.suggested_technique: Use linear forms in logarithms and Subspace-Theorem arguments for power sums or S-unit type equations.
framings.mapping_back: If one proves that ||r n_k - E_k|| cannot stay in [0,1) for infinitely many k unless r and the dominant characteristic roots satisfy exceptional algebraic relations, the original problem reduces to classifying those exceptional r.

framings.reframing: Treat floor(n r) as a coding of an irrational rotation and the selected indices n_k as a sparse sampling schedule. The question becomes whether a sparse rotation code can look rigid enough to collapse to a finite-dimensional recurrence.
framings.key_insight: Rigidity-sequence theory and sparse equidistribution on rotations or nilmanifolds suggest that most sparse schedules still spread mass rather than create repeated near-returns. A negative-space hypothesis is that recurrent subsequences would require n_k to behave like a rigidity sequence for the rotation by r.
framings.suggested_technique: Use rigidity-sequence criteria, sparse equidistribution estimates, and nilsequence comparison.
framings.mapping_back: Analyze {n_k r}. If those fractional parts remain equidistributed or sufficiently nonrigid, the bounded carry term cannot conspire with r n_k to satisfy a fixed recurrence.

framings.reframing: The graph {(n, floor(n r))} is a lattice slice in a width-1 strip, i.e. a model-set or cut-and-project picture. A recurrent subsequence would be a highly self-similar sub-pattern inside that quasicrystalline point set.
framings.key_insight: Model-set theory ties exact self-similarity to Pisot or substitution phenomena and Meyer-set rigidity. The negative-space guess is that only slopes supporting a hidden self-similar window could contain an infinite recurrence-compatible subset.
framings.suggested_technique: Use cut-and-project or model-set tools, Meyer-set criteria, and Pisot-scaling or substitution renormalization tests.
framings.mapping_back: Translate the selected points (n_k, floor(n_k r)) into a projected lattice subset. If no self-similar window or renormalization exists, rule out recurrence on geometric grounds.

framings.domain: geometry of numbers and lattice-point counting
framings.reframing: Study points (n_k, b_k) with b_k = floor(n_k r) as lattice points trapped in the strip 0 <= r x - y < 1. A recurrent subsequence becomes a structured parametric family of lattice points living forever in a strip of width 1.
framings.key_insight: Thin-sector and thin-strip counting results are sensitive to the Diophantine type of the slope. This suggests a negative-space hypothesis that recurrence-generated parametrizations cannot keep hitting such a strip infinitely often unless the slope has exceptionally tame approximation properties or the recurrence degenerates to polynomial growth.
framings.suggested_technique: Use lattice-point counting in thin sectors or tilted rectangles, discrepancy bounds, and parametric geometry-of-numbers estimates.
framings.mapping_back: Write the recurrence values as a structured curve k -> (n_k, b_k) and show that its intersection with the strip must be finite for generic r.

framings.reframing: Work in the structure of integers expanded by the Beatty graph or Beatty set for r. An infinite recurrence subsequence asks whether that structure interprets an infinite semilinear or module-like fragment inside {(n, floor(n r))}.
framings.key_insight: Presburger-definable sets are semilinear or ultimately periodic, while recent model-theoretic work on expansions by Beatty sequences isolates how much extra structure irrational floor maps add. The negative-space hypothesis is that any recurrent subsequence would force a definable periodic core that only very special slopes can support.
framings.suggested_technique: Use quantifier elimination or definability results for Beatty-sequence expansions together with Muchnik's definable criterion for Presburger definability.
framings.mapping_back: Formalize the recurrence relation and the selector set inside the Beatty expansion. If that would make the selector semilinear or ultimately periodic, compare with known non-Presburger behavior to exclude generic r.

framings.domain: additive combinatorics and higher-order Fourier analysis
framings.reframing: Reduce candidate subsequences modulo many q and ask whether k -> floor(n_k r) mod q exhibits the strong structured correlations characteristic of low-complexity linear recurrences.
framings.key_insight: Large Gowers U^d norms and inverse theorems detect hidden nilsequence structure. The negative-space hypothesis is that sparse samples of an irrational rotation remain too Gowers-uniform, across many moduli, to sustain a nontrivial recurrence.
framings.suggested_technique: Estimate Gowers norms or nilsequence correlations of floor(n_k r) modulo q and apply inverse theorems when the norms are large.
framings.mapping_back: If every modular reduction of any admissible subsequence looks higher-order uniform rather than nilsequence-like, then no fixed constant-coefficient recurrence can survive integrally.
